title: Fluid Dynamics & Viscosity — MCQs
description: Topics: Newton's formula for viscosity, laminar/turbulent flow & Reynolds number, Poiseuille's law, Stoke's law, continuity, Bernoulli, and numerical/conceptual problems.

questions.q: Newton's formula for viscosity relates shear stress τ to velocity gradient dv/dy. Which expression is correct?
questions.explanation: Newton's law of viscosity: shear stress τ = dynamic viscosity η × velocity gradient dv/dy.

questions.q: SI unit of dynamic (coefficient of) viscosity η is:
questions.explanation: Dynamic viscosity has units of force × time per area = N·s/m² = Pa·s.

questions.q: Coefficient of viscosity (η) physically represents:
options: Resistance to relative motion between fluid layers
questions.explanation: η quantifies internal friction — how strongly adjacent layers resist relative motion.

questions.q: Which best differentiates laminar from turbulent flow?
options: Laminar has smooth streamlines; turbulent has chaotic eddies
Laminar is faster; turbulent is always slower
Laminar occurs only in gases; turbulent only in liquids
questions.explanation: Laminar: orderly parallel layers; turbulent: random fluctuations and eddies.

questions.q: Which expression gives Reynolds number Re for flow in a pipe?
questions.explanation: Re = (ρ v D)/η (dynamic viscosity η) — a dimensionless quantity indicating inertial to viscous forces.

questions.q: For flow in a circular pipe, laminar flow typically occurs when Re is:
questions.explanation: Empirically, Re < ~2000 → laminar; Re > ~4000 → turbulent; between these is transitional.

questions.q: Poiseuille's formula for volumetric flow rate Q in a circular tube (laminar) is:
options: Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L)
Q = π r² ΔP / (4 η L)
questions.explanation: Poiseuille (Hagen-Poiseuille) for laminar viscous flow: Q = (π r⁴ ΔP)/(8 η L).

Stoke's law for drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid is:
questions.explanation: Stokes drag: F = 6π η r v valid for small Reynolds number (creeping flow).

questions.q: Terminal velocity v_t of a small sphere (Stokes regime) is given by:
questions.explanation: Balancing weight minus buoyancy with Stokes drag gives v_t = 2 r² (ρ_s - ρ_f) g /(9 η).

questions.q: A steel sphere (ρ = 7800 kg/m³) radius 1.0 mm falls in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) and attains terminal speed 0.05 m/s. Using Stoke's law, η ≈ ?
Equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid states:
questions.explanation: For incompressible flow mass conservation ⇒ volumetric flow conserved: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

questions.q: If pipe cross-section area is halved, what happens to flow speed (incompressible steady flow)?
questions.explanation: Q constant ⇒ v ∝ 1/A, so halving area doubles speed.

questions.q: Bernoulli's equation (inviscid steady flow) is:
options: p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along streamline
questions.explanation: Bernoulli: static pressure + dynamic pressure + hydrostatic head constant along streamline for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow.

questions.q: If velocity increases from v₁ to v₂ at same elevation, pressure change Δp (p₂ - p₁) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Bernoulli rearranged: p₂ - p₁ = ½ρ( v₁² - v₂² ) = -½ρ( v₂² - v₁² ).

questions.q: Liquid of density 1000 kg/m³ flows: v₁ = 2 m/s, v₂ = 5 m/s. Pressure difference p₂ - p₁ = ?
questions.explanation: Δp = -½ρ(v₂² - v₁²) = -0.5×1000×(25-4) = -10500 Pa (pressure drops where speed increases).

questions.q: Kinematic viscosity ν relates to dynamic viscosity η by:
questions.explanation: ν (m²/s) = η (Pa·s) / ρ (kg/m³).

questions.q: Reynolds number is dimensionless because:
options: It is a ratio of inertial to viscous forces
questions.explanation: Re = inertial forces / viscous forces — dimensionless by construction.

questions.q: Poiseuille's formula is valid for:
options: Steady laminar flow in circular tubes
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law assumes steady, incompressible, laminar, fully developed flow.

questions.q: Approximate dynamic viscosity of water at room temperature (20–25°C) is:
questions.explanation: η_water ≈ 1.0×10⁻³ Pa·s at room temperature.

questions.q: According to Poiseuille, if tube radius doubles, flow rate Q changes by factor:
questions.explanation: Q ∝ r⁴, doubling r gives 2⁴ = 16 times larger Q.

questions.q: Shear stress between fluid layers τ is related to viscosity and velocity gradient as:
questions.explanation: Newtonian fluids: τ = η (du/dy) where du/dy is velocity gradient perpendicular to flow.

questions.q: For most liquids, increasing temperature causes the dynamic viscosity to:
questions.explanation: Heating reduces intermolecular cohesive forces in liquids, lowering viscosity.

questions.q: Torricelli's theorem: speed of efflux from a small hole at depth h is approximately:
questions.explanation: From Bernoulli: v = √(2 g h) for efflux from a large reservoir; example: h=5 m → v≈7.07 m/s.

questions.q: In Stokes (creeping) flow regime the drag force on a small sphere is:
questions.explanation: Stokes drag F = 6π η r v is linear in v for low Reynolds numbers.

questions.q: Compute Re for water (ρ=1000 kg/m³, η=1.0×10⁻³ Pa·s) flowing at v=0.20 m/s in a pipe of diameter D=0.01 m:
questions.explanation: Re = ρ v D / η = 1000×0.2×0.01/1e-3 = 2000 (borderline laminar/transitional).

questions.explanation: Stokes regime (creeping flow) requires Re << 1 so inertial effects negligible.

questions.q: Which statement about turbulent flow is true?
options: It has high mixing and enhanced momentum transfer compared to laminar flow
It always has less drag than laminar flow
questions.explanation: Turbulence causes mixing and increased momentum/energy transfer; usually increases frictional losses.

questions.q: Viscosity causes pressure drop along a pipe because:
options: Viscous shear converts mechanical energy into heat, requiring extra pressure to maintain flow
questions.explanation: Viscous friction dissipates mechanical energy as heat; to maintain the same flow, a pressure gradient (ΔP/L) must do work against viscous forces.
